name: Moss
lede: Moss is the yellowish, softly greyed green of the plant that carpets stones and trees, a color word that dictionaries define by the plant and paint catalogues borrowed for several different mixed greens.

sections.title: The plant and the word
sections.body:
Moss as a color is the plant's color and little more. Paterson's dictionary calls moss simply a shade of green, moss green a yellowy-green or olivy green, and moss-grey a greeny-grey [1]. St Clair's glossary of color names agrees: yellowed green, the color of moss [2].

It works best as a comparison word, a reference green. Finlay describes a naturally coloured cotton boll, an unexpected aqua green, as sea turquoise mixed with moss and mint [4]. He also lists *moss tone* among the evocative names that Pantone added to its expanded system [3]. In our sources the earliest English record of *moss green* is 1884, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 atlas gives 1905 for *moss* [5].

sections.title: A name for several mixed greens
sections.body:
In the nineteenth-century paint trade, *moss green* was a bought color, but not one pigment. Linke and Adam (1913), as reported in the Pigment Compendium, list moss green with oil green, olive green, bronze green and silk green as trade names for chrome-green mixtures made mostly from smaragd green (chromium oxide hydrate), zinc yellow and a little barite white [6].

The books disagree about what it was. The Compendium notes that one source lists moss green as a less common name for emerald green, while another, Mayer in 1991, says it is the same as chrome green [7]. A tube labelled moss green could therefore be quite different things, which is a good reason to treat the word as a color and not as a material [6][7]. Compare [[sap-green]] and [[viridian]], which do name materials.

sections.title: Two mosses
sections.body:
The swatch is a mid-light, yellowish green, `#8A9A5B`, falling in block 120 of the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, which that system calls moderate yellow green [5]. A look-alike called [[moss-green]] sits almost on top of it in our data, and neighbors include [[sage]], [[olive]], [[lichen-green]] and [[mossy-green]] [5].

Not every source agrees on how dark moss is. The library records the German RAL standard's 6005, named moss green, with a screen value near `#0F4336`, a deep bluish green far darker than this swatch [5]. Other sources in the library give mosses closer to our swatch, which is why the page uses the plain, yellowed green that Paterson and St Clair describe [1][2][5].

sections.title: In Japan
sections.body: Our library files two Japanese traditional colors under English moss words [8]. *Bright moss* renders Hiwamo'egi, "siskin sprout yellow", a sharp yellow-green, and *dusty moss* renders Usu'ao, "pale blue", a muted grey-green [8]. Another Japanese name, Yanagizome ("willow-dyed"), sits on this very swatch [8]. The English words are our glosses, not translations, and the Japanese names are the traditional ones [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 164 works, or 0.7 per cent [9]. It is almost absent before the nineteenth century: none of the 1,388 paintings from the 1100s to the 1400s hold it, and only 4 of 2,231 from the 1500s do [9]. It rises to 86 of 8,345 in the 1800s and 46 of 1,674 in the 1900s, nearly four times the museums' baseline [9]. Inside a painting it is a middle tone about half the time and a highlight 45 per cent of the time, so it tends to be a color of foliage in light, not of shadow [9].

The devoted painters are of the 1880s and after: [[painter:georges-seurat|Seurat]] holds it in 8 of his 41 works here, Camille Pissarro in 7 of 50 [9]. The largest covers are mostly landscapes and gardens, among them Berthe Morisot's [[painting:nga-52194|Girl in a Boat with Geese]] (1889) and Bonnard's [[painting:commons-Q17492969|The Large Garden]] (1895) [9]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike color, not a pigment test [9]. Where to look: in a landscape painting, find the pale foliage that is yellow and grey at once, and you have found moss [9].
